solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Party leads to some sleep deprivation — have kip wherever suits (4,4)

indicators.note: the leads of the next words are their first letters

blocks.note: first letters of some, sleep, deprivation

annotation.surface: A party that leads to sleep loss, so guests nap wherever they can.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash hides where the definition starts: 'have' is wordplay, and 'kip wherever suits' is the definition. Kip is British slang for sleep.
annotation.definitionFit: To doss down is to bed down for the night in whatever makeshift place is available.

clue.text: Having dreadful ado, counts old silver coins (9)

indicators.note: the letters of the fodder are in a dreadful state, so rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone making a fuss while counting an old coin collection.
annotation.walkthrough: A ducatoon was a silver coin of 17th-century Italy and the Low Countries, a larger cousin of the ducat.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical term: the ducatoon was a silver coin once current in Italy and the Low Countries.

clue.text: Husband cutting pig up in display (4,3)

indicators.note: the husband cuts into the pig, so sits inside it

blocks.note: a sow is a female pig
as with a race that is up and running, the runners are off

annotation.surface: A husband carving up a pig in front of an audience.
annotation.walkthrough: The pig is SOW, not HOG, and 'up' is not a reversal here but a word of its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to parade something so others admire it is to display it.

clue.text: Bores medic with misfortunes (6)

annotation.surface: A doctor who tediously bores everyone with tales of woe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bores' reads as a noun for tedious people, but it is the verb: to make holes.
annotation.definitionFit: To drill is to bore a hole.

clue.text: Before permission to act, decree resolution (9)

indicators.note: the decree comes before the permission

blocks.note: a will is a decree or command

annotation.surface: A legal decree being resolved once authority to act is granted.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is written back to front: the first piece named, 'permission to act', goes second.
annotation.definitionFit: Willpower is resolution, the determination to carry something through.

clue.text: Historian VIP boastfully backtracks (6)

indicators.note: the whole string goes back the way it came

blocks.note: a nob is a toff, a bigwig

annotation.surface: A pompous dignitary retreating from something he boasted about.
annotation.walkthrough: Edward Gibbon wrote The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire; 'Historian' could also be a monkey in disguise.
annotation.definitionFit: Edward Gibbon was the 18th-century English historian.

clue.text: Avarice besetting fringes of The Met (7)

indicators.note: greed surrounds the other letters
the fringes of a word are its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Greed surrounding the Metropolitan Opera or the Met Police.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Met' looks like one name, but only 'The' is wordplay; 'Met' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: welcoming someone on arrival is meeting them.

clue.text: Café from Egon Ronay initially in club (9)

indicators.note: take the initial letters of Egon Ronay
those letters go inside the club

blocks.note: a brassie is an old golf club, a wooden two-wood

annotation.surface: A café recommended by the famous restaurant guide, found in a club.
annotation.walkthrough: Egon Ronay was a food critic whose guides rated British restaurants, which suits the café surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: the French word for an informal restaurant serving simple food and drink, much like a café.

clue.text: Such unity could make no sense (7)

indicators.note: the fodder's letters could be made into the answer

annotation.surface: A cynic's remark that such perfect unity makes no sense.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Such' points on to the answer: unity of the kind this anagram produces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the state of being one whole is unity, and 'such' points at the answer as its kind.

clue.text: Expanded odourless gas that’s odd (3)

indicators.note: the formula is written out in full, the 2 becoming a second O

blocks.note: carbon dioxide, whose formula has one carbon and two oxygens

annotation.surface: A puzzled note about an odourless gas that has expanded.
annotation.walkthrough: Carbon dioxide is CO2; 'expanded' writes the second oxygen out. 'Coo!' is a British exclamation of surprise.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Coo!' is what you say when something strikes you as odd.

clue.text: Ignorant, stupid, endless repeat (10)

indicators.note: the word loses both its ends

blocks.note: SILLY without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A string of insults: ignorant, stupid, the same thing over and over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endless' could clip only the last letter; here SILLY loses both ends to give ILL.
annotation.definitionFit: Illiterate can mean ignorant in general, not only unable to read.

clue.text: Writer wants time cut in part (8)

indicators.note: the cut goes inside the part

annotation.surface: An author wanting a time cut in his part.
annotation.walkthrough: Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire books.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Victorian novelist Anthony Trollope, author of the Barsetshire books.

clue.text: Decoration left on piece of armour plate (6)

indicators.note: in an across clue, left is added on after the armour

blocks.note: a tasse is a plate of armour guarding the thigh

annotation.surface: An ornament left on a suit of armour.
annotation.walkthrough: The obscure part is the armour: a tasse (or tace) is one of the overlapping plates hanging below the breastplate.
annotation.definitionFit: A tassel is a decorative tuft of threads.

clue.text: Former king leading away from answer (4)

indicators.note: the first piece leads, coming before the second

annotation.surface: A deposed monarch leading people away from an answer.
annotation.walkthrough: Offa was the 8th-century king of Mercia, famous for Offa's Dyke on the Welsh border.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Anglo-Saxon ruler of Mercia, who died in 796.

clue.text: Skill needs past struggling (9)

indicators.note: the letters thrash about into a new order

annotation.surface: A struggler told that acquiring skill takes getting past something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Needs past' reads as grammar in the surface, but those two words are exactly the letters to shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: being adept at something means having skill in it.

clue.text: Bearing ordinary pot plant (5,5)

annotation.surface: An ordinary potted plant bearing something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pot plant' looks like a houseplant; 'pot' is cannabis, which is also grass.
annotation.definitionFit: Sword grass is a grass or sedge with sharp, blade-like leaves.

clue.text: Again investigate case of rogue despot once found in river (2-7)

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside letters
the despot is found inside the river

blocks.note: first and last letters of ROGUE
the Exe, a river in Devon
Idi Amin, former dictator of Uganda

annotation.surface: A fresh inquiry into a rogue former dictator discovered in a river.
annotation.walkthrough: Idi Amin ruled Uganda in the 1970s, hence 'despot once'; the Exe runs through Exeter in south-west England.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with the prefix doing the work of 'again': to look into something a second time.

clue.text: Brazen criminal hassles me (9)

indicators.note: the letters are criminally mistreated, so rearranged

annotation.surface: A complaint that a brazen crook keeps pestering the speaker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brazen criminal' reads as one phrase, but 'Brazen' is the definition and 'criminal' the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone brazen acts boldly with no sense of shame.

clue.text: Rose finally seduces number one bachelor in German city (5,5)

indicators.note: take the final letter of seduces
the bachelor goes inside the city

blocks.note: 'number one' is a nursery euphemism for a wee

annotation.surface: Rose at last seduces the leading bachelor in a German city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name; it is the flower. 'Number one' is not first place but a child's word for a wee.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: eglantine, a European wild rose with fragrant leaves.

clue.text: Most of timber on northern island suitable for court? (7)

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter, so the timber is cut short
in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

annotation.surface: Timber on a northern island that might be fit for a law court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court or a tennis court; the question mark signals the old sense of courting, or wooing.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone wooable is fit to be courted.

clue.text: Ring secures inverted support gear used in lift? (7)

indicators.note: the ring holds the other piece inside it
the support is turned upside down, reading upwards

blocks.note: to ring is to bell, a call on the phone
a bra is a support garment

annotation.surface: A ring holding a support upside down in a lift mechanism.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'lift' as weightlifting rather than an elevator.
annotation.definitionFit: A barbell is the bar of weights used in weightlifting.

clue.text: Two books, each absorbing day after day (4)

indicators.note: each takes the days inside it

annotation.surface: Two books each absorbing the reader day after day.
annotation.walkthrough: There are two Eddas, the Elder (Poetic) and the Younger (Prose), collections of Old Norse writing.
annotation.definitionFit: The Edda is the name shared by two Icelandic books of Norse myth and poetry.

clue.text: One destined to serve picked up drink and MDMA (7)

indicators.note: what is picked up is heard, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: a draught is a drink; E is ecstasy, the drug MDMA

annotation.surface: A conscript caught with a drink and ecstasy.
annotation.walkthrough: Draught is the British spelling for a drink from the barrel; said aloud it sounds like the American DRAFT.
annotation.definitionFit: A draftee is someone conscripted for military service.

clue.text: Fungus source beginning to rot in huge borders of grass (6)

indicators.note: take the beginning of rot
that letter goes inside huge
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Where mushrooms spring up: rot among huge grassy margins.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fungus' is not a mushroom but Fungus the Bogeyman, the picture book by Raymond Briggs, who is its source.
annotation.definitionFit: Raymond Briggs created Fungus the Bogeyman.

clue.text: First sign of jungle animal’s pad (6)

indicators.note: take the first letter of jungle

blocks.note: the otter, with 's as the link 'is'

annotation.surface: The first trace of a jungle beast's paw print, or its lair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pad' could be an animal's paw or home; here it is a notepad. The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mainly British: a small book of paper for jotting notes on is a pad.

clue.text: Attitude in estate, maybe one overwhelmed by anger (8)

indicators.note: an estate is one example of a car
the one is swallowed up by the anger, so sits inside it

blocks.note: an estate is a type of car, a station wagon

annotation.surface: A stance adopted on a country estate by someone consumed by fury.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Estate' suggests land; in Britain an estate is also a car with a large boot, called a station wagon elsewhere.
annotation.definitionFit: Carriage is posture, the way one holds oneself, which is one sense of attitude.

clue.text: English look back into human form of cultivation? (10)

indicators.note: to look back is to face the way you came, so the word for look is read in reverse
both pieces go inside the human

annotation.surface: An Englishman peering back into how people cultivate things.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags an odd definition: bees are kept and cultivated rather than crops.
annotation.definitionFit: Beekeeping is a form of husbandry, cultivating bees for honey.

clue.text: Traitorous secret agents progressively picked out letter (3)

indicators.note: take letter one of the first word, letter two of the second, letter three of the third

annotation.surface: Double agents gradually exposed by an intercepted letter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picked out' suggests taking first letters; 'progressively' moves one letter further along in each word.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword-friendly sense: letters have spelt-out names, and the twentieth letter's name is written this way.

clue.text: Receptacle, somewhat useless, eventually returned (6)

indicators.note: only part of the words is used
those letters read back the other way

blocks.note: the run of letters inside useLESS EVentually

annotation.surface: A container that proved rather useless and was eventually sent back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' is easy to read as a hedge on 'useless'; it is the signal that the answer sits inside the next words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a jug, bowl or cask is a container for holding liquid.

clue.text: Revise opinion on fools — simpletons, primarily (8)

indicators.note: take the first letter of simpletons

annotation.surface: Changing one's mind about fools, who are mainly simpletons.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' is not a link here but RE, the memo word for 'about'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: judging something afresh is revising your view of it.
